eventops.title: EventOps
eventops.summary: Calendar, staff and finances for your events company.
eventops.metaTitle: EventOps: management system for event companies
eventops.metaDescription: EventOps brings the calendar, clients, staff and finances of an event company into a single system. A ShippersLab own product, in production.

features.title: Calendar
features.body: All events for the month, week or day in a single view, with the site visit, setup, sound check and teardown of each one.

features.title: Quotes
features.body: Pick services from your list and the total adds up on its own. The quote is exported as a PDF with your logo, ready to send to the client.

features.title: Staff
features.body: Add team members to each date with their role and see who is free before assigning them, so no event is left short-handed.

features.title: Finances
features.body: Deposits and installments in pesos or dollars, per-event and general expenses, and a monthly summary of income and expenses. All the data can be exported to CSV.

features.title: Clients
features.body: Each client with contact details, source, history and next event. Individuals, companies and venues in a single record.

features.title: Team
features.body: Everyone at the company signs in with their own user. Invitations are sent by email and each company only sees its own data.

eventops.lead: The calendar, clients, staff and finances of your event company in a single system. A ShippersLab own product, in production.
eventops.overview: An event company handles dates, teams, clients and payments all at once. When that information is scattered across spreadsheets and messages, it is easy for two events to overlap, for staff to be missing, or for nobody to know exactly how much money came in and how much is still owed.
eventops.approach: EventOps brings the whole operation into a single system. Each event has its client, its team and its money movements, and the calendar shows at a glance what needs to happen and when. We designed it around how an event company works, so everyone always sees the same information.
eventops.flowDescription: Each event is entered once and everything else comes from it. Nothing has to be copied into another spreadsheet.

flow.title: Create the event
flow.body: The event is created with its client and related dates are added: site visit, setup, sound check and teardown. They all show up in the calendar and the system warns when two dates overlap.

flow.title: Build the quote
flow.body: Services such as sound, lighting or an LED screen are picked from the list and the total is calculated automatically. The quote downloads as a PDF with the company logo.

flow.title: Assign the staff
flow.body: For each date, the team members who will work are added with their role, showing who is free and how many are still missing.

flow.title: Collect and track
flow.body: The deposit, installments and event expenses are recorded, in pesos or dollars. At month end, the summary shows what came in, what went out and what is still pending.

audience.intro: For small businesses with stock, orders or bookings run on Excel, WhatsApp or an old system. If you're losing time entering the same data twice, we start there.

examples.title: What it looks like in different businesses.

items.title: Distributor or wholesaler
items.body: Orders come in over WhatsApp, inventory lives in an Excel file and nobody's quite sure what's in the warehouse. An inventory and sales system can update stock when an order is confirmed and show you what to restock before you run out.

items.title: Appointment-based business
items.body: In a clinic, a repair shop or a beauty salon, the schedule often lives in a notebook or on one person's phone. A booking system brings together the team's calendar, each client's history and the day's payments.

items.title: Event company
items.body: Dates, crew and payments spread across chats and spreadsheets. That's what EventOps solves: a calendar with site visits, setup and teardown, clients with their history, crew assigned per date and each month's results.

process.title: How we work and how we quote.

steps.title: A 30-minute call
steps.body: What gets entered, who enters it and where things get stuck. That tells us where to start.

steps.title: A scope document
steps.body: What's in, what's out, what it costs and when it'll be ready. All clear before we start.

steps.title: Partial deliveries every week
steps.body: If the system is large, we split it up and start with what hurts most, like inventory or orders. Every week you see a working piece and try it with your team.

steps.title: Rollout
steps.body: We roll it out with your team and adjust it based on real use.

pricing.label: Price and timeline
pricing.body: They depend on how many parts the system has and what it needs to connect to. If you already pay for hosting or other services, we use them. If not, we handle them and charge their cost plus a management fee.

afterDelivery.label: Warranty
afterDelivery.body: If a bug turns up on our side, we fix it under warranty.

afterDelivery.label: Maintenance
afterDelivery.body: Optional, for changes and improvements after launch. Without it, the project costs less.

afterDelivery.label: Your data
afterDelivery.body: It's confidential and we only use it for your project.

items.question: Should I get a custom system or an off-the-shelf one?
items.answer: If an off-the-shelf system fits how you work, it may be enough. A custom system makes sense when your operation has its own steps that packaged software doesn't cover, or when you end up using three programs and a spreadsheet to fill the gaps. In the first conversation we tell you what we think fits your case.

items.question: I run everything on Excel today. What happens to that data?
items.answer: We start from there. We move your product, client or order spreadsheets into the new system, and that's planned in the proposal. If a spreadsheet still works for you, we can keep it connected.

items.question: Will my team be able to use it?
items.answer: We build it around how your team works, and they test it every week while it's being built. If you want, we add a training session so everyone can use it from day one.

items.question: Who owns the system, and what happens to my data?
items.answer: Your data is confidential and we only use it for your project. Who owns the code depends on whether it's a custom build or one of our products like EventOps. We put it in writing in the proposal before we start.

faq.title: Questions about websites, booking pages and catalogs.

items.question: Can I update prices and products myself?
items.answer: We can add a dashboard so you can edit prices, photos and products without depending on anyone. We define it in the proposal based on how often your catalog changes.

items.question: How is this different from opening a store on an e-commerce platform?
items.answer: E-commerce platforms make sense if you want checkout with a cart and automated shipping. If your customers already buy from you on WhatsApp, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering is usually simpler: they pick, message you with the order ready, and you keep selling the way you always have. We help you figure out which one fits.

items.question: Can the booking page send reminders?
items.answer: It can be included. Reminders, cancellations and rescheduling are defined in the proposal based on what your business needs.

items.question: Will the site show up on Google?
items.answer: We build it so Google can read it properly: every page with its own title, description and content, and fast on mobile. Ranking high takes time and depends on how many people search for what you offer. We do not promise rankings.

items.question: I already have an old website. Do you rebuild it or fix it?
items.answer: It depends on how it was built. We take a look, and if improving it makes more sense than starting over, we say so in the proposal.

covers.title: What we solve.
covers.body: The repeated questions that eat your day: hours, prices, stock, open slots. The bot answers what it can and escalates what it cannot. AI where it pays off, not for show.

audience.title: Who it is for.
audience.intro: For businesses that get a lot of questions and cannot reply on time. If your team spends hours on the same answers every day, a well-built bot takes that load off.

items.title: Shops that sell on WhatsApp
items.body: The same stock, price and shipping questions, all day long.

items.title: Appointment-based businesses

items.title: Event companies

examples.title: What a bot can do for your business.

items.title: Shop that sells on WhatsApp
items.body: People ask all day whether something is in stock, how much it costs and whether you ship. A bot can answer with your catalog and prices, take the order and pass it to you to close payment or arrange delivery.

items.title: Appointment-based business
items.body: The bot shows open slots, books the appointment and confirms it on WhatsApp. If someone asks for something unusual, it lets you know so you can reply yourself.

items.title: Event company
items.body: Inquiries about dates and quotes arrive after hours. The bot collects the basics, like date, venue, guest count and service, and leaves the inquiry ready for you to quote.

faq.title: Questions about bots and AI agents.

items.question: Does it work with my current WhatsApp number?
items.answer: It depends on how you use that number today. We assess each case and walk you through the options before we start.

items.question: What if the bot says something wrong?
items.answer: The bot answers with the information we give it: your prices, your hours, your catalog. If it does not know something, it says so and hands the conversation to you. You test it before your customers ever see it.

items.question: What is the difference between a bot and an AI agent?
items.answer: A bot follows a set path, with menus, options and fixed answers. An AI agent understands what the customer writes in their own words and can take actions, like checking your stock or booking an appointment. We use AI where it helps resolve the request, and a simple bot when that is enough.

items.question: Can I see the conversations and reply myself?
items.answer: It can be added depending on the project, for example an inbox to review what the bot said or a direct handoff to your WhatsApp. We define it in the proposal.

items.question: Does it replace my support team?
items.answer: It takes care of the repetitive questions so your team can focus on what needs a person: a complaint, a large sale, a special case.

integraciones.metaDescription: Custom integrations with Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA invoicing, AI WhatsApp bots and Google Sheets. Enter data once. Scope in writing.
integraciones.h1: Custom integrations with your current tools.
integraciones.lead: We connect Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA invoicing, WhatsApp and your spreadsheets to each other. Enter something once and it shows up where it should, without tearing down what already works.

covers.title: What we solve.
covers.body: Data that moves by hand from one place to another: an order that comes in on WhatsApp and gets typed into a spreadsheet, a sale you collect in one place and invoice in another. We connect those pieces so the data is entered once and nobody has to copy it.

items.title: Mercado Pago: payments and reconciliation
items.body: Every payment that comes in through Mercado Pago can be recorded automatically in your spreadsheet or system, linked to its order. Reconciliation stops being a line-by-line review at the end of the month, and you see right away what is paid and what is pending.

items.title: Tiendanube: stock and orders
items.body: If you sell online and in a physical shop, there should be a single stock. We sync Tiendanube inventory with your spreadsheet or system and make each new order reach whoever prepares it, without checking the dashboard.

items.title: ARCA electronic invoicing
items.body: We connect your sales to ARCA (formerly AFIP) electronic invoicing services so the invoice is issued automatically when a payment or order is confirmed. You set the rules: which receipt type, for whom and when.

items.title: AI WhatsApp bot
items.body: A WhatsApp assistant that answers common questions, takes orders or bookings and records them where they belong. When a conversation needs a person, it hands it over. We build it with your answers and your rules, not generic scripts.

items.title: Google Sheets and CRM
items.body: If your team works in Google Sheets or a CRM, we use it as the hub: orders, payments and contacts from other tools arrive there organized, and changes you make there are reflected wherever needed.

process.title: How we work and how we quote.

steps.title: A 30-minute call
steps.body: We look at how data moves today: where it comes in, where it gets copied by hand and where it gets lost. That shows which connection saves you the most work.

steps.title: A scope document
steps.body: What gets connected, what happens if something fails and what we need from you. Price and timeline in writing before we start.

steps.title: Partial deliveries every week
steps.body: We connect each tool through its official API, and every week you test a working piece with your real cases.

steps.title: Rollout
steps.body: We leave it running with your team. Every integration alerts you when something does not go as expected.

pricing.label: Price and timeline
pricing.body: We charge an implementation fee based on the complexity of the integration and, once it is running, a maintenance fee. Some tools charge for their own usage: if you already have the accounts, we use them; if not, we handle them and charge you their cost.

afterDelivery.label: Warranty
afterDelivery.body: If an integration fails because of a bug on our side, we fix it under warranty.

afterDelivery.label: Maintenance
afterDelivery.body: Covers the adjustments when an external tool changes how it connects. Without it, that adjustment is on you.

afterDelivery.label: Your data
afterDelivery.body: It's confidential and we only use it for your project.

items.question: Which tools can you connect?
items.answer: WhatsApp, Google Sheets, Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA electronic invoicing and CRMs, among other tools that offer a way to connect from outside (an API). If yours does not, we look at it in our first conversation and tell you the alternatives.

items.question: Can you connect ARCA (formerly AFIP) electronic invoicing?
items.answer: Yes. We connect your sales to ARCA so each invoice is issued without entering it by hand. In our first conversation we go over which account details are needed and help you set them up.

items.question: What happens if an integration breaks?
items.answer: We build every integration to alert you when something fails. If the bug is ours, we fix it. If an external tool you chose changes how it connects, the adjustment is on you, unless you have a maintenance plan with us.

items.question: Should I do this or build a new system?
items.answer: If what you use today works and the problem is moving data by hand, connecting is usually faster and cheaper. If your tools no longer give you what you need, a management system may make more sense. We tell you in the first conversation.

items.question: Can't I just do this myself with Zapier or Make?
items.answer: For simple connections, yes, and sometimes that is what we recommend. When there are rules specific to your business, many steps or high volume, it pays to have something custom built that you can control.

como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.title: Does your business need a website? How to know if it is worth it
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.metaTitle: Does your business need a website? How to know if it is worth it
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.metaDescription: Signs a website makes sense for your small business or shop, when it does not yet, and how to measure whether yours works. With a checklist and FAQ.
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.excerpt: Concrete signs to decide whether a website adds value to your business, when it is better to wait and how to measure whether yours is working.
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.answer: A website is worth it if people look for you on Google, if you answer the same questions all day on WhatsApp or Instagram, if you have products or services to show or if your customers need to trust you before buying. It can wait if all your customers come through referrals and you can barely keep up, if you are still testing what to sell or if you will not be able to keep the information up to date. In the meantime, a complete Google Business Profile and a WhatsApp Business catalog may be enough.
intro: Many businesses in Argentina sell well with Instagram, WhatsApp and word of mouth. So the question comes up: do you need a website, or is it just another expense? The honest answer is that it depends. A website does not sell on its own, but in some cases it saves you time, brings in inquiries you are losing today and builds trust with people who do not know you yet.
In this guide you will find concrete signs to help you decide, the cases where it is better to wait and how to measure whether the website you already have is doing its job.

sections.title: Signs a website makes sense
paragraphs: If two or more of these sound familiar, a website will probably help:
items: People look for you on Google. If someone types your business name, or something like «hardware store in Rosario», and cannot find you, those inquiries go somewhere else. A website with your information, together with a Google Business Profile, makes you show up when people search.

You answer the same questions all day. If on WhatsApp or Instagram you keep replying about prices, opening hours, delivery areas or payment methods, a website with that information gives you time back and lets customers start the conversation almost decided.
You have products or services to show. An organized catalog with photos, descriptions and prices or ranges is easier to browse than an Instagram feed or a set of PDFs you send by chat.

You need to build trust. Many customers, especially other businesses, look up your website before writing or paying. Seeing who is behind it, where you are, how you work and how to reach you lowers their doubts.
You depend on a single social network. If your account gets blocked tomorrow or the algorithm changes, you lose your storefront. A website is a place of your own that you control.
You want to take orders, bookings or inquiries without being on top of it. A form, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering or a booking system keep working while you are busy with something else.

sections.title: When you do not need one yet
paragraphs: A website is not always the priority. It can wait if:
items: All your customers come through referrals and you can barely keep up with the orders you already have.
You are still testing what to sell or to whom, and your offer changes every week.
You will not be able to keep the information up to date. A website with old prices or a phone number nobody answers does more harm than having nothing.
sections.closing: In those cases, a complete Google Business Profile and a good WhatsApp Business catalog may be enough for now. When the business grows or you find yourself answering the same things over and over, ask the question again.

sections.title: Summary: when a website helps and when it can wait
paragraphs: This table puts the two lists above side by side so you can compare them at a glance:

table.caption: When a website helps a business and when it can wait

rows.label: How people find you
cells: People search for your name or what you sell on Google.
All your customers come through referrals.

rows.label: Chat inquiries
cells: You answer the same things all day: prices, opening hours, delivery or payment methods.
You can barely keep up with the orders you already have.

rows.label: What you offer
cells: You have products or services that are easier to understand with photos and descriptions.
You are still testing what to sell or to whom, and it changes every week.

rows.label: Trust and channels
cells: Customers look you up before writing or paying, or you depend on a single social network.
A Google Business Profile and a WhatsApp Business catalog are enough for now.

rows.label: Upkeep
cells: You can keep prices, catalog and contact details up to date.
You will not be able to update the information. An outdated website does more harm than having nothing.

sections.title: How to know if your current website works
paragraphs: If you already have a website, existing is not enough. Here are four simple ways to check whether it is doing its job:
items: Impressions and clicks in Google Search Console. It is a free Google tool that shows how many times you appeared in results (impressions), how many people clicked through (clicks) and for which searches. If you have almost no impressions, Google is not showing you. If you have impressions but few clicks, review the title and description of your pages.

Inquiries coming from the website. Ask every new customer how they found you, or use a form or a WhatsApp link that only lives on the website so you know which inquiries come from it. In the end, what matters is whether the website brings you conversations.
Speed. If the page is slow to load, many people leave before seeing it. You can measure it for free with Google PageSpeed Insights, which also tells you what is slowing it down.
How it looks on a phone. Many people will visit from their phone. Open it on yours: can you read it without zooming? Are the buttons easy to tap? Can you find the WhatsApp or phone number in seconds?
sections.closing: If the answer to any of these is «no» or «I do not know», that is where to start.

sections.title: What a website needs to be worth it
paragraphs: A useful website for a small business or shop does not need to be big. It needs to quickly answer the questions people ask you by chat today: what you do, for whom, where, how much (even if it is a range or a starting price) and how to contact you.

If it also has an up-to-date catalog, a visible WhatsApp button and loads fast on a phone, it already covers what most customers will look for. Everything else can be added later, once you know which pages people visit and which inquiries it brings.

link.label: See how we build websites and catalogs

checklist.title: Quick checklist
checklist.intro: Before deciding, go through this list:
items: Do people search for my business or what I sell on Google?
Do I answer the same questions several times a day?
Do I have products or services that are easier to understand with photos and descriptions?
Do my customers need to trust me before buying or paying in advance?
Do I depend on a single social network to be found?
Will I be able to keep the information up to date?
If I already have a website: do I know how many impressions, clicks and inquiries it brings?
checklist.closing: If you said yes to several of the first five and also to the sixth, a website is probably worth it.

items.question: Is Instagram enough instead of a website?
items.answer: For many businesses it is a good start. The difference is that the Instagram account is not yours and Google does not always show it when someone searches for what you sell. A website and social media complement each other: social media creates interest and the website organizes the information and makes you findable.

items.question: How long does a new website take to show up on Google?
items.answer: There is no fixed timeline and it depends on each site. It helps to add it to Google Search Console, submit the sitemap and have a Google Business Profile that links to the website. Search Console shows you when the first impressions start to appear.

items.question: Do I need a catalog with a shopping cart?
items.answer: Not always. If you sell few products or each sale needs a conversation, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering is usually enough. An online store with payments makes sense when the number of orders justifies it.

items.question: What if I already have a website but it brings no inquiries?
items.answer: Check the basics first: whether it shows up in Search Console, whether it loads fast, whether it looks good on a phone and whether contact details are visible. Often the website does not answer what customers are looking for, or it is hard to reach you from there.

items.question: Does a website replace WhatsApp?
items.answer: No, it complements it. The idea is that the website answers the usual questions so the WhatsApp conversation starts with an informed customer.

como-organizar-una-empresa-de-eventos.excerpt: How an event production company moved from one Excel file of clients, dates and cash to a single system, and how an event runs in EventOps today.
como-organizar-una-empresa-de-eventos.answer: Organizing an event company takes one place for the calendar, the crew, the quotes and the cash. An Excel file for an event company gets messy once there are several dates, setup and teardown, deposits and quotes at the same time. A system for sound and lighting producers enters the event once, and the calendar, the PDF, the payments and the expenses come from that. EventOps is that software for event companies: ShippersLab builds it in Argentina for ARS 50,000 a month, on a single plan, with one free week.
intro: If you run a sound, lighting or event company, Excel is often enough at the start: dates, clients and cash in one file. You still have to quote, set up, collect the deposit and know who is going.
This post covers how one event production company left that spreadsheet for a single system, and how an event runs in EventOps today.

sections.title: What falls apart when everything lives in Excel
paragraphs: An event production company arrived with no calendar. Clients, dates and cash flow all sat in one Excel file.
From that base, everything the trade needs hangs off the same sheet:
items: The site visit, the setup, the event and the teardown have to be read between rows, because there is no calendar of their own.
A date that overlaps another one has to be spotted by eye before you confirm.
The crew for setup and teardown is not tied to that date, and the pay is calculated separately.
The deposit and what is still owed get mixed in with the rest of the numbers.
The quote is built in another file and sent to the client by hand.

sections.title: How EventOps started
paragraphs: EventOps started with a specific request: an event production company asked us to quote a calendar, a client list and cash flow. While building it we saw that every sound, lighting and event company has the same problem, so we turned it into our own product, now in production.
The calendar was the visible part. What had to be modeled was crew pay, and the money of each event, which in the spreadsheet was mixed in with everything else.

sections.title: What an event looks like on the calendar
paragraphs: Today the event is entered once. Related dates are added and they all show up on the calendar. If two dates overlap in time, EventOps warns you before you confirm.

image.alt: EventOps demo showing a wedding's site visit, setup, event and teardown, each with its day and time.
image.caption: Sample wedding dates on the public EventOps demo.

items: Related dates. A meeting, a sound check or another date can be added alongside the site visit, the setup and the teardown.
Statuses. Quote, reserved with a deposit, confirmed, done and cancelled. Each one has its own color on the grid.
Views. Month, week, day or agenda. To reschedule, you drag the event to another day.

sections.title: Crew cost: setup, teardown and extra hours
paragraphs: The hardest part was crew cost. This company paid per setup and per teardown, and sometimes paid more when the hours ran over.
In EventOps each role has a fixed amount per stage (setup, teardown or site visit) or an hourly rate. When you assign someone, the amount fills in on its own.

image.alt: EventOps demo showing a wedding's technicians, DJ and driver, with who is assigned and who is still missing.
image.caption: Crew for a sample wedding. The names are from the public demo.

items: Assignment by date. Each person comes in with a role: technician, DJ, lighting or driver.
Who is free. Before you add someone, you can see if they already have another date that day.
Pay per stage or per hour. The fixed amount covers setup or teardown. The hourly rate covers it when the time runs long.

sections.title: The quote comes out as a PDF
paragraphs: The quote is built from the event, using services from your list. The total calculates itself. The PDF downloads with your logo, ready to send on WhatsApp or by email.

image.alt: PDF quote from the EventOps demo, with sound, lighting and DJ services.
image.caption: Sample PDF from eventops.digital/presupuestos, built from the service list.

items: From the catalog. Each service brings a name, what it includes, a base price and a unit: per event, per day, per hour or per unit.
Adjustments. You can change the quantity and the price, add a free item and apply a discount or a surcharge.
Pesos or dollars. The quote is in ARS or USD. If the event already has payments, the currency stays fixed.
PDF with your logo. A quote for the client, a proforma, a setup sheet and a receipt for each payment. The invoice is issued separately: these PDFs have no tax validity.

sections.title: Deposits, expenses and the month in numbers
paragraphs: From the total you collect a deposit and split the balance into the installments you agree, in pesos or in dollars. Each payment is marked, you can see what is left, and the receipt comes out as a PDF.
Crew, equipment rental and supplies go on the event or stay as a general expense. The month shows income, expenses and net, with pesos and dollars kept apart. Movements can be exported to CSV.

image.alt: PDF proposal page from the EventOps demo, with the total amount and the scope of the service.
image.caption: The terms page of the same PDF: total amount and scope. The amounts are sample figures.

Site visit, setup, event and teardown are on the calendar, and it warns you if two dates overlap.

A fixed amount per stage or an hourly rate. When you assign someone, the pay fills in on its own.

cells: The deposit and the balance get mixed in with other numbers.
The deposit and the installments stay on the event, in pesos or in dollars.

rows.label: Quotes
cells: Built in another file and sent however you can.
Comes out as a PDF with your logo, from your services, with the total calculated.

rows.label: Cash flow
cells: Income and expenses for the month have to be rebuilt.
Event or general expenses, and the month in pesos and dollars kept apart.

sections.title: When EventOps fits as it is
paragraphs: EventOps fits as it is if you run events, you have crew to assign and you send quotes. There is a single plan, ARS 50,000 a month, with one free week.
If the operation is something else, such as stock, orders or appointments, that is built to fit.
items: Events with site visit, setup and teardown on the same calendar.
Crew in charge, with a role and pay per stage or per hour.
Quotes as PDF, and a deposit or installments for the balance.
The month's cash in pesos and in dollars, kept apart.
sections.closing: If those four describe how you work, start with the trial week.

checklist.intro: Go through this list before you add another sheet:
items: Do dates, clients and cash live in the same Excel file?
Do I pay setup and teardown per stage, and sometimes more when the hours run over?
Do I build every quote by hand to send it on WhatsApp?
Do I collect a deposit and installments, and not always know what each event still owes?
Do I need to see who is free before I confirm a date?
Is my work running events, with crew in charge and quotes for the client?
checklist.closing: If several answers are yes, a system for this trade will do more than another sheet in the same file.

items.question: Is Excel enough for an event company?
items.answer: It is enough while there are few dates and the same person always looks at them. When the calendar, the crew, the deposits and the quotes share the spreadsheet, a system makes sense: the event is entered once and the calendar, the PDF, the payments and the expenses come from that.

items.question: What should a system for sound and lighting producers cover?
items.answer: A calendar with site visit, setup and teardown, crew with a role and pay, a PDF quote, and the event's cash: deposit, installments and expenses, in pesos or in dollars.

items.question: Does EventOps fit as it is?
items.answer: It fits as it is if you run events, you have crew to assign and you send quotes. If the operation is stock, orders or appointments, that is built to fit.

cuanto-cuesta-un-sistema-de-gestion-a-me.title: What a custom management system costs a small business
cuanto-cuesta-un-sistema-de-gestion-a-me.metaTitle: What a custom management system costs a small business
cuanto-cuesta-un-sistema-de-gestion-a-me.metaDescription: What drives the price of a custom management system: modules, users, integrations and moving off Excel. Scope and price agreed in writing.
cuanto-cuesta-un-sistema-de-gestion-a-me.excerpt: What pushes the price of a custom management system, which costs sit outside the build, and what to bring to the first conversation so the quote can close.
cuanto-cuesta-un-sistema-de-gestion-a-me.answer: The price of a custom management system depends on the modules and screens, the users and permissions, the integrations, moving the data out of Excel, and the reports. We do not publish a rate: the price is built from the scope of your operation and agreed in writing, together with that scope, before we start. Here is how that price is put together.
intro: If the business runs on Excel and you are asking for a quote, the figure on its own is not enough. You need to know what goes into the system and what stays out, because that is what the price comes from.

This note covers what drives it, which costs are worth looking at apart from the build, how it compares with staying on a spreadsheet or buying off-the-shelf software, and what to bring to the first conversation.

sections.title: What drives the price
paragraphs: The price depends on the system. Tidying up inventory is not the same job as adding orders, cash, role permissions and a close for the accountant. The name of the trade does not say how much work there is.

That is why there is no published rate. The proposal states the scope, and the price follows that scope. It does not come from a catalog of loose screens: the parts are looked at together, because a short flow with no integrations is not the same work as one with permissions, a heavy migration and closing reports.

A distributor that wants an order to reduce stock is not asking for the same thing as a booking business that wants the team's schedule and the day's takings. The screens look similar from far away. The rules do not. These are the parts that move the price the most:
items: Modules and screens. Each part of the operation that goes in, such as inventory, orders, cash, bookings or clients, adds screens, states and rules. A short path is not the same work as an operation with several stages and exceptions.

Users and permissions. One person signing in is not the same as each role seeing and doing something different. Owner, admin, warehouse or branch changes what has to be built and what each person can touch.

Integrations. Connecting invoicing, payments, email or an API is work on top of the screens. If the tool has a clear way for data to go in and out, that is what we use. If it does not, we define how the information travels.

Migration from Excel. Moving products, clients or movements is not copying the spreadsheet. Names have to be unified, duplicates resolved, and you decide which history comes along. If a spreadsheet still works for you, it can stay out or stay connected.

Reports. A list is not a close. If you need to see what is still unpaid, what to restock or how the cash closed, that is designed with the same rules your team already uses, not with a generic dashboard.
sections.closing: If the system is large, it can be split so we start with what hurts most, such as inventory or orders. What goes into this stage and what waits also goes in writing, so the price does not mix work that will be done with work that will not.

sections.title: Costs worth knowing apart from the build
paragraphs: The build is one part of the quote. Some costs are worth seeing beside it, named, so they do not show up later. They do not change how we quote: they are separated from the system.
They go in the proposal only if the system needs them. If they are not needed, they are not added to fill out a list.
items: Server, domain and accounts. If you already have a server, a domain, the WhatsApp API or an AI model, we use them. If you do not, we manage them and charge the cost plus management.
Maintenance. It is optional. It covers changes and adjustments once the system is running. Without maintenance, the project costs less.
Training. It is optional too. If you want a session so your team learns to use it, it is added. If you do not hire it, the project costs less.
Bugs in the system. If the fault is ours, we fix it. That does not depend on having hired maintenance.
Changes in an external API. If an API you chose changes and you did not hire support, you pay for that fix. It is not covered by the build.
Your data. It is confidential. We use it to build the system and, if you hire maintenance, to maintain it.
sections.closing: The document separates what the system is, what is optional and which external services are used or managed. You can choose the build without dragging the rest along.

sections.title: Excel, off-the-shelf, or custom
paragraphs: The first conversation usually brings up the same comparison: stay in Excel, adopt off-the-shelf software, or commission a custom system. There is no option that fits every small business. It depends on how specific the operation is and on whether the team can work the way the program already works.
The table is qualitative. It does not replace a quote and it does not hide figures. The actual price comes from the scope, in writing.

table.caption: Excel, off-the-shelf software and a custom system: upfront cost, ongoing cost, fit to the process and who maintains it

rows.label: Upfront cost
cells: The spreadsheet is already there. What it takes is the time to build it and to rebuild it when it falls short.
You use the product that already exists. The limit shows up when the operation needs something that plan does not include.
It is the agreed build. It grows with the modules, the permissions, the integrations and the data to move.

rows.label: Ongoing cost
cells: The spreadsheet license, if there is one, and the time of whoever keeps it up to date.
A subscription while you use it. If it falls short, another program appears or you go back to Excel.
Maintenance is optional. Server, domain or APIs are charged separately when they have to be managed.

rows.label: Fit to the process
cells: It bends to how you work, until the formulas, the copies and the loose files cannot keep up.
The team adapts to the program. What does not fit stays in a patch or in another tool.
It is built around how your team works, with the rules they already use.

rows.label: Who maintains it
cells: Someone on your team. If that person is away, it is hard to reconstruct where each piece of data ended up.
Whoever makes the product. You can ask for what the product allows, not a flow it does not contemplate.
If you hire maintenance, we keep going with it. We still fix our own bugs.

sections.title: How to ask for a quote properly
paragraphs: A closed quote comes from understanding the operation, not from a short message with the name of the trade. The clearer you arrive at the first conversation, the less back and forth it takes to write the scope and the price.

You do not need a tidy document. It is enough to show how you work today. The order is simple: we listen to the operation, we write what is in and what is out, and the price goes in that same document, before we start. Maintenance, training and external services sit on another line, so they are visible apart.
items: A real case. Pick an order, a booking or a stock movement and walk through it from the moment it comes in until it is paid or delivered.
The spreadsheets. Even if they are messy. That is where columns, states and data entered in more than one place show up.
Who does what. Who enters data, who approves, who looks at the cash and who should not see costs or margins.
What it has to connect to. Invoicing, payments, email, WhatsApp or another tool. If you already have the account or the API, say so in the conversation.
What hurts today. The part that gets stuck, gets lost or gets argued about. If the system is large, that is where we start.
What stays out. Saying what is not in this stage keeps the price from mixing in work that is not going to be done yet.
sections.closing: From that we write the document: what gets built, what does not, what we need from you, what the implementation costs and what maintenance costs. It is agreed in writing before we start. We do not publish a typical timeline. The time also depends on the system and it lives in that document, not in a generic promise.

sections.title: Signs that custom is the right fit
paragraphs: Off-the-shelf software is enough when the operation fits what that program already does and the team can work that way, without a spreadsheet beside it. A custom system makes sense when the way of working has its own steps and the gap is held together with Excel and messages.

An events company, the first client, ran everything in Excel: cash flow, clients and no calendar. They asked for a quote for a calendar, client management and cash flow. The system that came out of that work is EventOps, and it covers more than the original request: the event is entered once, and the calendar, the quote, the payments and the expenses come from that. How an event runs there is told in the note on organizing an events company.

That case is not a template to copy. It shows the difference between quoting a screen and looking at the whole operation. If your business does something else, the scope is written for that operation, not for another trade.
items: Your own rules. Discounts, states, deposits or exceptions that off-the-shelf software cannot model without patches or a spreadsheet beside it.
Split data. The same thing is entered in Excel, in chat and in another program, and nobody fully trusts a single list.
Different permissions. Not everyone on the team should see costs, margins or the cash, and today that is solved by hiding columns.
You already went back to the spreadsheet. You tried off-the-shelf software and the daily work stayed in Excel, because the operation did not fit.
It has to talk to what you already chose. Invoicing, payments or an API, using your accounts if you already have them.
sections.closing: If the off-the-shelf product covers the day to day and your team uses it without a parallel spreadsheet, there is no need to replace it. In the first conversation we say what looks like the better fit for your case, and the scope is written before there is a price.

checklist.title: Quick checklist
checklist.intro: Before the first conversation, go through this:
items: Can I walk through an order, a booking or a stock movement from start to finish?
Do I have the spreadsheets at hand, even if they are messy?
Do I know who enters data, who approves and who should not see each piece of data?
Do I know what it has to connect to, and whether those accounts already exist?
Can I say what goes into this stage and what stays out?
Does the off-the-shelf program I looked at let me work the way I work today, or does it push me back to Excel?
checklist.closing: If you can answer the first ones, the conversation is enough to write scope and price. If the last one is also yes, it is worth looking at a custom system before stretching the spreadsheet.

items.question: Is there a reference price for a custom system?
items.answer: We do not publish a rate. The price depends on the system: modules and screens, users and permissions, integrations, migration from Excel and reports. Scope and price are agreed in writing before we start.

items.question: Are maintenance and training required?
items.answer: No. Maintenance and training are optional. Without them, the project costs less. If the bug is in the system we built, we fix it anyway.

items.question: What if I already have a server, a domain or WhatsApp?
items.answer: We use them. If you do not have them, we manage them and charge the cost plus management. The same applies to an AI model when the system needs one.

items.question: Who pays if an external API changes?
items.answer: If the fault is ours, we fix it. If an API you chose changes and you did not hire support, you pay for that fix.

items.question: What happens to my business data?
items.answer: It is confidential. We use it to build the system and, if you hire maintenance, to maintain it. Which spreadsheets are migrated, and which are not, is written in the proposal.
